headline: Keisha Lance Bottoms says Democrats better spend big on the South
author: Erin Doherty

paragraphs.text: Georgia Democratic Gov.-elect Keisha Lance Bottoms said the midterm election results “have spoken for themselves” in showing the need for the Democratic Party to invest more in the South.

“I would hope that in two years, we're not having to beg and borrow to be able to run successful campaigns,” Bottoms said in an onstage interview at the POLITICO Pub on the sidelines of the National Governors Association’s New Governors Leadership Forum in Utah.

Democrats had a historically strong cycle in Georgia this year: Bottoms became the first Democrat to win her state’s governorship in more than a quarter-century, Democratic Sen. Jon Ossoff won reelection handily, and the party flipped the state House for the first time in more than two decades. But it wasn’t just Georgia. Democrats also won Senate seats in North Carolina, South Carolina and Mississippi, three states that have long been out of reach for the party, and just missed in Louisiana.
“The numbers have been there for Democrats to flip that seat in Mississippi for a while, but the investment has not been there,” Bottoms said.
She said that her campaign was a lean operation, particularly in contrast to her GOP opponent’s. Rick Jackson spent nearly $200 million of his own money on his campaign.

“During the primary it was the shoestring, dental floss campaign, we were holding it together with every single thing that we had because we weren't getting in the resources and some people have written Georgia off,” she said.

“But also even when those resources come from our friends nationally: Trust us. Nobody knows their community, nobody knows their electorate better than the people who are living and breathing it every single day.”
Bottoms made history as the first-ever Black woman ever elected governor to in the U.S. earlier this month. But on her campaign trail, she did not focus on the historic nature of her candidacy.

“I wake up as a Black woman every day,” she said. “So it was not something that I felt compelled to talk about, it was never top of mind, so it was not even a conscious decision for me not to talk about it. I just didn’t think about it.”
She said she instead focused on voters’ cost of living concerns that dominated the cycle.

“For me, it was about focusing on the issues. I can't hide, and don't want to hide, that I'm a Black woman,” she said. “To the extent that the conversations were organic with me as a mother or as a woman or whatever the case may have been, then it was a part of the discussion. But I can tell you, as I moved around the state of Georgia, people were focused on, ‘what are you gonna do about this cost of living? How are you going to make my life better?’”
